title: Matthew emphasizes enduring commandments
observation: Matthew's Jesus denies abolishing the Law and associates doing and teaching commandments with standing in the kingdom.
alternateReading: Matthew's fulfilment language can refer to the arrival of the kingdom and a new authoritative interpretation rather than an unqualified requirement that every Torah rule binds all later Gentile followers.
limitation: This is Matthew's literary presentation of Jesus; the historical occasion and relation to later Gentile communities are reconstructed, not independently observed.

title: Galatians assigns the Law a changed role
observation: Paul describes the Law's custodial role as bounded by the coming of faith and strongly resists circumcision being imposed on Gentile Christ-followers.
alternateReading: The target may be Gentile entry into Abraham's promise rather than a universal declaration that Jews must abandon Torah observance.
limitation: The precise applicability of Paul's argument to Jewish observance remains debated; the Thiessen source was checked at abstract level only.

title: Paul also upholds and positively describes the Law
observation: Romans 3:31 rejects nullifying the Law; Romans 7:12 calls the commandment holy; Romans 13 and Galatians 5 connect love with the Law's fulfillment.
alternateReading: These affirmations need not imply that Paul requires all Gentiles to observe every Mosaic regulation; 'fulfill' and 'establish' require argument-specific interpretation.
limitation: A simple 'Jesus keeps Law; Paul rejects Law' thesis omits contrary Pauline passages.

title: Mark's food-purity passage has a contested reading
observation: Mark 7 reports a dispute about handwashing, tradition, and defilement. The Greek phrase in 7:19c has been taken as an explanatory gloss that Jesus declared all foods clean.
alternateReading: Logan Williams argues that the phrase belongs to Jesus' digestive explanation, relating the debate to ritual impurity rather than a repeal of prohibited animals.
limitation: Competing grammatical analyses and translation punctuation must be stated; Mark 7 cannot simply be equated with abolition of all food laws.

title: Acts 15 and Galatians 2 narrate the dispute differently
observation: Acts presents communal deliberation and a formal decision concerning Gentiles, while Paul describes a meeting focused on his Gentile gospel and a later public disagreement with Peter.
alternateReading: Some interpreters harmonize the meetings as different perspectives on the same event; others consider separate meetings or editorial shaping.
limitation: Acts is a later narrative; it should not be quoted as Paul's unmediated report. Historical identity and sequencing of the meetings are debated.

title: Different meanings of obligation may explain part of the tension
observation: The texts speak about continuity of scripture, how God's promises reach fulfillment, inclusion of Gentiles, and moral transformation; these are not necessarily identical questions.
alternateReading: Matthew's insistence on even minor commandments can still represent a genuine disagreement with claims that all followers are released from specific Torah obligations.
limitation: Romans 10:4 uses telos, whose interpretation as end, goal or culmination varies. A reconciled reading is a hypothesis, not proof that there is no theological tension.

title: The call to relinquish possessions in the rich-ruler encounter
observation: Mark portrays Jesus instructing one wealthy man to sell his possessions, give to the poor, and follow; the later teaching also describes wealth as a serious impediment to entering the kingdom.
alternateReading: The imperative is addressed to a particular person, not stated as a uniform accounting rule for every follower. Yet its placement within broader discipleship teaching makes it difficult to dismiss as irrelevant beyond that encounter.
limitation: Matthew and Luke contain versions of a related Gospel tradition, not three independent verbatim historical transcripts. Shively is a pastoral commentator and her application is not a consensus judgment.

title: Luke emphasizes poverty and eschatological reversal
observation: In Luke, the teaching on the plain addresses the poor and the rich with opposing blessings and woes, while further accounts criticize hoarding, urge almsgiving, and portray a rich person ignoring someone in need.
alternateReading: Some interpret Luke's poverty language chiefly as disciples' dependence on God or as an anticipated reversal rather than a blanket claim that material poverty is itself virtuous and wealth itself always culpable.
limitation: Ndekha offers a contextually framed panegyric reading with modern Malawian application; this is one argued reading. Luke's descriptions should not automatically be generalized to all four Gospels.

title: Matthew 25 ties judgment to acts of care, but the beneficiaries are debated
observation: Matthew portrays the Son of Man relating treatment of hungry, thirsty, stranger, unclothed, sick and imprisoned people to treatment of himself.
alternateReading: Scholars disagree whether 'the least of these my brothers' refers particularly to Jesus' disciples or emissaries, to needy people in general, or to a deliberately wider ethical horizon that connects both.
limitation: A contested audience/beneficiary identification prevents direct inference of a universal civil welfare policy or a claim that charity alone exhausts Matthew's theology of judgment.

title: Paul's collection seeks practical relief and reciprocity
observation: Paul organizes contributions across communities and speaks of matching current abundance to others' shortage with an aim of equality; Romans identifies the poor among Jerusalem believers as recipients.
alternateReading: The scope is an interchurch project, not a proposed model for state redistribution or a complete prescription for how Christians should organize all property. Interpretations of equality differ.
limitation: Barclay's article is examined in full; Welborn's contribution is drawn only from the publisher abstract and must not be cited for unseen arguments or pages.

title: Paul's appeal is substantial but distinguishes advice, capacity, and willingness
observation: In 2 Corinthians 8:8 Paul describes his appeal as not a command; 8:12 concerns one's means and 8:13 avoids transferring distress; 9:7 opposes grudging or compelled contributions.
alternateReading: Paul's noncoercive rhetoric can nonetheless create strong communal expectations, and his Macedonian example celebrates giving out of poverty. The difference from the rich-ruler demand need not signal rejection of Jesus' ethic.
limitation: Paul's emphasis on a specific fundraising situation and Jesus' challenge to a specific person are not parallel commands addressed to the same audience. Barclay warns that such texts can be abused to pressure poor donors.

title: Solidarity with the poor appears explicitly in Paul's undisputed letters
observation: Galatians 2:10 reports a request to remember the poor, Romans 12 urges sharing with believers in need, and the collection is portrayed as a multi-community commitment to material support.
alternateReading: Some of these beneficiaries are identified specifically as fellow believers, especially in Jerusalem. That narrower reference does not automatically establish Paul's position on poverty outside the churches.
limitation: The collection's explicit target cannot by itself prove either that Paul denied assistance to nonbelievers or that he taught an unlimited universal redistribution policy.

title: The widow's offering can signify devotion while raising exploitation concerns
observation: Jesus observes a poor widow contributing from her livelihood immediately after criticism of scribes who exploit widows. The nearby anointing episode also contests assumptions about how costly gifts should be evaluated.
alternateReading: Some readings commend the widow as an exemplar of self-giving, while others emphasize the indictment of a system that consumes vulnerable people's resources. Kubiś's abstract argues for a positive reading while acknowledging a negative one.
limitation: The article's abstract was inspected, not its full analysis; the narrator records the widow's action, not Jesus ordering impoverished people to surrender their last resources.

title: Luke narrates substantial restitution without a uniform dispossession formula
observation: Luke reports Zacchaeus pledging half his property to the poor and restitution for wrongdoing, alongside the rich ruler's distinct call to sell all and the disciples' broader instruction to give alms.
alternateReading: Zacchaeus's episode is narrative description rather than a general rule that giving exactly half suffices; juxtaposition may show Luke's emphasis on concrete generosity and repentance in differing situations.
limitation: The sources do not supply a single formula for the appropriate percentage of wealth to give. Different audiences, genres, and sequences matter.

title: Acts depicts communal sharing but is a separate narrative source
observation: Acts describes property-sharing among an early Jerusalem community; Paul's letters independently document an organized transfer of resources from other assemblies toward believers in need.
alternateReading: Acts' community portrait may serve a theological and literary ideal, so its details should not be uncritically equated with Paul's independent letters or interpreted as proof of an identical economic institution.
limitation: Acts 4's narrated practices cannot be attributed as direct instructions spoken by Jesus or as Paul's first-person eyewitness report.

title: Named women participate in Jesus' ministry and learning
observation: Luke names women accompanying and supporting the ministry, depicts Mary listening as a disciple, and John portrays a Samaritan woman whose testimony draws hearers.
alternateReading: Narrated financial support, learning and public testimony do not by themselves prove a later institutional office or that the Gospel writers opposed every gender distinction.
limitation: These texts are literary portrayals with different theological aims. A narrative event should not be treated as a universal office regulation.

title: Women are integral to resurrection narratives
observation: Mark describes women at the execution and burial; Luke and Matthew report women's tomb experience and witness, and John has Jesus direct Mary Magdalene to inform the disciples.
alternateReading: The evangelists differ in who is present, who speaks, how the encounter unfolds and how their testimony is received. A witness commission and later ecclesiastical ordination are not synonymous.
limitation: Mark 16:9–20 is excluded from this claim due to its disputed longer ending. The shorter Mark narrative's conclusion must not be silently blended with John and Matthew.

title: Romans 16 presents women as significant participants
observation: Paul commends Phoebe using diakonos and prostatis, refers to Prisca and Aquila as fellow workers, and names Mary and Junia among respected figures in his networks.
alternateReading: The range of diakonos, prostatis and labor/coworker terms does not map exactly onto later titles such as ordained deacon, bishop or priest. Modern office labels require further evidence.
limitation: Sybrandi's open article argues for substantial women's ministries; its full ecclesiological inference is an interpretation, not a direct transcript of Roman congregational appointments.

title: Junia's apostolic identification remains contested
observation: Romans 16:7 names Junia and Andronicus in a phrase commonly rendered 'notable among the apostles,' but the syntax of the expression has been contested.
alternateReading: Sybrandi argues reception history obscured Junia's apostolic standing. Burer and Wallace's published abstract proposes the sense 'well known to the apostles' rather than inclusion among them.
limitation: Burer and Wallace's full argument was not inspected. Neither view should be presented as a textual certainty, and 'apostle' itself may not imply a later episcopal office.

title: 1 Corinthians 11 assumes women pray and prophesy
observation: In the same undisputed letter, 11:5 assumes women pray and prophesy while 14:34–35 appears to require silence in assemblies; the larger chapter regulates disruptive or competing speech.
alternateReading: Some scholars restrict 14:34–35 to particular types of speech (questioning, evaluating prophecy, or disruptive interruption), distinguish different assembly contexts, or read the lines as a Corinthian position corrected in verse 36.
limitation: The text of 11:5 regulates women's appearance as well as presuming speech; it should not be represented as a straightforward statement of modern equality. Baum's article is only accessible here at summary level.

title: 1 Corinthians 14:34–35 has a meaningful placement variant
observation: Some Western textual witnesses move verses 34–35 to after verse 40 instead of the usual position after 33. Scholars offer insertion, rhetorical-quotation and contextual-authenticity accounts.
alternateReading: Niccum stresses external manuscript evidence and argues that displacement alone cannot establish an interpolation; Wilson supports quotation/refutation and offers a different account of the Western displacement.
limitation: The extant manuscript evidence is not the same thing as proving an original text or speaker. No presently known continuous manuscript lacks the two verses altogether; this pilot has not examined a full critical apparatus.

title: 1 Timothy's restriction is a distinct and disputed Pauline witness
observation: 1 Timothy 2:11–15 instructs women to learn quietly and restricts teaching or exercising authority over a man; Titus 2 also specifies domestic-related instruction by older women.
alternateReading: Some argue that teaching/authority restrictions are enduring and tied to creation, while others interpret the instruction against local teaching disorders, relational conflict, or the rare Greek verb authentein.
limitation: The Pastorals' authorship is seriously disputed and must not be collapsed into unchallenged speech from Paul. The modern denominational report is explicitly confessional, not neutral scholarly arbitration.

title: Galatians 3:28 informs equality debates without answering every office question
observation: Paul asserts unity in Christ across male/female, slave/free and Jew/Gentile distinctions in a discussion of baptism, inheritance and Abraham's promise.
alternateReading: Some readings interpret unity as equal spiritual standing with continuing gendered church functions; others argue that equality in status also challenges exclusion from participation and authority.
limitation: Tolmie surveys divergent scholarly positions rather than proving a single application. Galatians 3:28 does not itself describe the administrative structure of an assembly.

title: Acts and Paul's coworker references require separate source categories
observation: Acts portrays Priscilla and Aquila teaching Apollos, while Paul's letters independently refer to Euodia and Syntyche as gospel coworkers and to Prisca and Aquila hosting an assembly.
alternateReading: A historical reconstruction may use these accounts as complementary evidence, but Acts is a later literary witness and house-hosting, teaching in a narrative, and preaching are not interchangeable titles.
limitation: Claims about ordained offices cannot be inferred from a single coworker, host, or teaching label without reconstructing how those activities related to contemporary assemblies.

title: A universal gender conclusion cannot rest on one isolated text
observation: The canonical corpus both portrays substantial female agency and preserves texts restricting certain forms of speech or authority; they have different genres, audiences and authorship profiles.
alternateReading: Complementarian, egalitarian, situational and redactional readings each integrate these sources differently. Treating any one set as decisive without addressing contrary passages leaves the comparison incomplete.
limitation: A historical claim about Jesus' views cannot be inferred simply by equating a Gospel narrator's approval of women with a later church office; modern ecclesial regulations also require explicit theological decisions.

title: Both corpora reject personal retaliation
observation: Jesus commands enemy love; Paul rejects repayment of evil and urges blessing persecutors.
alternateReading: These instructions may differ in rhetorical scope and concrete application.
limitation: Shared interpersonal ethics do not settle the legitimacy of public coercion.

title: Punitive authority and enemy love
observation: Romans describes rulers exercising punitive authority, while Matthew instructs disciples against retaliation.
alternateReading: Paul may distinguish governmental functions from the conduct of individual disciples.
limitation: Romans does not explicitly authorize disciples to occupy coercive offices.

title: Paul explicitly invokes the Lord's instruction
observation: Paul attributes a prohibition of marital separation to the Lord, consistent with the restrictive Markan tradition.
alternateReading: The precise transmitted saying known to Paul need not match Mark verbatim.
limitation: The written Gospel and Pauline letter are distinct historical witnesses.

title: Abandonment and exceptions
observation: Paul permits departure by an unbelieving spouse and describes the believer as not enslaved.
alternateReading: Permission to accept separation may not entail permission to remarry.
limitation: The meaning of bondage and Matthew's exception require linguistic review.

title: Both corpora recognize community discipline
observation: Matthew describes escalating responses to wrongdoing; Paul directs exclusion in a specific misconduct case.
alternateReading: The procedures and grounds for exclusion differ across the two settings.
limitation: Neither passage supplies a comprehensive modern safeguarding policy.

title: Repeated forgiveness and restoration
observation: Jesus urges repeated forgiveness; Paul urges comfort and renewed love after punishment.
alternateReading: Luke explicitly mentions repentance while Paul's immediate concern is excessive sorrow.
limitation: The identity of the offender in the two Corinthian letters is disputed.

title: Judgment criteria and justification
observation: Matthew depicts judgment involving treatment of others; Paul contrasts justification with works of the Law.
alternateReading: Final judgment and justification may describe distinct but related dimensions of salvation.
limitation: The referent of the least ones and scope of works of the Law remain debated.

title: Paul also recognizes judgment involving deeds
observation: John and Paul describe accountability involving conduct; Galatians connects faith and love.
alternateReading: Romans 2 may function rhetorically as a standard exposing human failure.
limitation: The passages do not establish a single causal model of salvation.

title: Service and humility
observation: Mark rejects domination among disciples; Philippians commends humility and Philemon favors appeal.
alternateReading: Paul's appeal can still carry substantial social pressure.
limitation: Rhetorical claims of voluntary action do not prove absence of coercion.

title: Authority and institutional power
observation: Matthew criticizes status seeking while Paul exercises disciplinary authority and recognizes leaders.
alternateReading: Authority exercised as service need not conflict with the rejection of domination.
limitation: Ancient assembly roles cannot be equated directly with modern clergy offices.

title: Mission scope changes
observation: Matthew narrates an Israel-focused initial mission and a later universal commission; Paul describes Gentile mission recognition.
alternateReading: The universal commission may reflect later movement development rather than independently confirm historical sequence.
limitation: Literary chronology is distinct from historical chronology.

title: Prayer motivation and communal practice
observation: Matthew criticizes prayer for recognition; Paul encourages prayer and regulates assembly conduct.
alternateReading: Private prayer instructions may be read more strictly than a critique of motivation.
limitation: Neither text directly addresses modern state-sponsored religious practice.

title: Status reversal and legal freedom
observation: Mark reverses status rankings; Galatians asserts unity and Philemon urges brotherly reception.
alternateReading: Theological equality may undermine hierarchy without explicitly requiring legal abolition.
limitation: Philemon does not unambiguously demand manumission.

title: Ancient slavery and accommodation
observation: Luke uses household servants as imagery; Paul addresses enslaved persons within existing social arrangements.
alternateReading: Paul's counsel may favor obtaining freedom or making use of existing circumstances.
limitation: The syntax of 1 Corinthians 7:21 and historical slavery contexts require specialist review.

title: Resurrection affirmed
observation: Mark affirms resurrection against the Sadducees; Paul argues that resurrection is integral to Christian proclamation.
alternateReading: The two arguments address different objections and do not establish identical resurrection models.
limitation: Neither passage specifies every feature of resurrected existence.

title: Transformation of resurrected life
observation: Luke describes changed marriage arrangements; Paul describes a transformed resurrection body.
alternateReading: The spiritual body need not imply an immaterial or disembodied existence.
limitation: Greek terminology and ancient resurrection traditions require specialist review.

title: Uncertain timing and vigilance
observation: Mark warns that the hour is unknown; Paul depicts the day of the Lord arriving unexpectedly.
alternateReading: The warnings may concern different audiences or stages of eschatological events.
limitation: Shared vigilance does not resolve the chronology of the expected events.

title: Expectation within a generation
observation: Matthew includes a generation saying; Paul uses first-person plural language for living believers at the coming.
alternateReading: The generation referent and Paul's rhetorical identification with living believers are disputed.
limitation: Neither wording alone establishes an unconditional date prediction.

title: Sexual conduct and discipleship
observation: Matthew addresses adultery and desire; Paul grounds sexual conduct in bodily belonging to Christ.
alternateReading: The passages address distinct acts and ethical rationales rather than identical rules.
limitation: Ancient sexual terminology does not map automatically onto modern categories.

title: Specific communal rules
observation: Mark addresses divorce and remarriage; Paul treats misconduct and mixed-belief marriages.
alternateReading: Paul may extend rather than contradict earlier teaching when addressing new cases.
limitation: Silence in a Gospel passage cannot establish opposition to a Pauline rule.

title: Endurance amid suffering and hope
observation: Jesus blesses persecuted followers and urges perseverance; Paul contrasts suffering with future glory.
alternateReading: Paul develops a wider account of suffering than persecution alone.
limitation: The texts do not imply that all preventable suffering should be accepted.

title: Responding to opposition
observation: Matthew anticipates hostility toward disciples; Paul calls for blessing persecutors and rejecting revenge.
alternateReading: Matthew's mission instructions and Paul's community ethics address different situations.
limitation: The selected passages do not provide exhaustive guidance for self-protection.

title: Jesus and divine agency
observation: John describes the Son's life-giving role; Paul links Christ with creation and exaltation.
alternateReading: Divine identity, delegated agency and exaltation are competing interpretive frameworks.
limitation: Later creedal terminology cannot be assumed to exhaust the original meanings.

title: Relationship to the Father
observation: John describes access to the Father through Jesus; Paul describes the Son's ultimate subjection to God.
alternateReading: Functional subordination and claims about divine nature need not be identical questions.
limitation: The passages do not independently settle later metaphysical disputes.

title: Redemptive significance of death
observation: Mark uses ransom imagery; Paul connects Christ's death with redemption and release from the curse.
alternateReading: Different metaphors may express overlapping claims without a single atonement mechanism.
limitation: The Greek terms and their historical contexts require further study.

title: Forgiveness and redemption
observation: Gospel narratives depict forgiveness and salvation before the crucifixion; Paul connects redemption with Christ's death.
alternateReading: Narrative chronology does not exclude a theological account of the death's significance.
limitation: The passages do not specify a uniform causal theory of forgiveness.

title: Inclusion across boundaries
observation: Luke discourages excluding an outsider acting in Jesus' name; Matthew and Paul extend participation across nations or ethnic groups.
alternateReading: Ethnic inclusion and recognition of outsiders do not necessarily imply religious pluralism.
limitation: The outsider's action in Jesus' name limits the scope of the example.

title: Christ-centered access
observation: John presents Jesus as the way to the Father; Romans frames justification through faith in its Christ-centered argument.
alternateReading: The texts address different questions about access and justification.
limitation: Neither selected passage alone settles the fate of all non-Christians.

title: Distributed spiritual activity
observation: Luke depicts authority granted to disciples; Paul describes diverse gifts among community members.
alternateReading: Mission authority and assembly gifts need not refer to identical phenomena.
limitation: Narrative reports and community instructions have different evidential functions.

title: Limits and priorities of gifts
observation: Luke narrates disciples' inability to heal; Paul prioritizes love and regulates assembly contributions.
alternateReading: The passages address different limitations rather than a unified theory of miracles.
limitation: They do not establish guaranteed healing or settle the duration of spiritual gifts.

title: Jesus rejects oath-taking in Matthew 5
observation: Jesus rejects oath-taking in Matthew 5; Paul invokes God as witness to his assertions.
alternateReading: Paul may use solemn assurances rather than the oath practices targeted by Matthew.
limitation: The exact scope of the prohibition and ancient conventions require verification.

title: Matthew emphasizes reliable ordinary speech
observation: Matthew emphasizes reliable ordinary speech; Paul defends the sincerity of his dealings with Corinth.
alternateReading: Paul's defense is situational rather than a general prohibition of deceptive speech.
limitation: Shared concern for credibility does not establish identical rules about oaths.

title: Luke reverses seating-related honor
observation: Luke reverses seating-related honor; Philippians urges regard for others and invokes Christ's humility.
alternateReading: The meal illustration and Christological example operate in different social settings.
limitation: Neither passage alone resolves the legitimacy of formal leadership positions.

title: Jesus challenges greatness rankings
observation: Jesus challenges greatness rankings; Paul challenges boasting and urges sober self-assessment.
alternateReading: Differentiated gifts may still support unequal responsibilities within communities.
limitation: The texts do not establish a comprehensive modern theory of social equality.

title: The Gospel illustration and Romans both challenge judgment that ignores one's own wrongdoing
observation: The Gospel illustration and Romans both challenge judgment that ignores one's own wrongdoing.
alternateReading: Romans may address a rhetorical interlocutor rather than a universal audience directly.
limitation: The target and scope of judgment must be assessed in each literary context.

title: Luke contrasts self-righteousness with humility
observation: Luke contrasts self-righteousness with humility; Paul urges the Corinthians to examine themselves.
alternateReading: Paul's test concerns faith and apostolic controversy rather than precisely the same moral failure.
limitation: The common emphasis on self-assessment does not erase differing purposes.

title: Jesus challenges a Sabbath accusation
observation: Jesus challenges a Sabbath accusation; Romans permits differing convictions about days and foods.
alternateReading: Paul may address practices distinct from the Sabbath controversy in Luke.
limitation: The identity of the disputed days and the role of Torah require further study.

title: Jesus prioritizes release from suffering
observation: Jesus prioritizes release from suffering; Paul urges restraint where liberty could harm another.
alternateReading: Paul's conscience argument is not identical to Jesus' defense of Sabbath healing.
limitation: The kinds of harm and the religious obligations involved differ.

title: The Samaritan illustration challenges restrictive neighbor categories
observation: The Samaritan illustration challenges restrictive neighbor categories; Paul limits internal discipline to insiders.
alternateReading: A distinction in disciplinary jurisdiction can coexist with concern for outsiders.
limitation: Neither text alone determines all membership or exclusion practices.

title: Jesus rejects stopping an outsider acting in his name
observation: Jesus rejects stopping an outsider acting in his name; Paul urges appropriate conduct toward outsiders.
alternateReading: The outsider categories are not identical: one concerns an exorcist, the other broader social relations.
limitation: These passages do not establish unrestricted acceptance of every external practice.

title: Jesus permits hospitality for mission workers
observation: Jesus permits hospitality for mission workers; Paul defends material support for proclaimers.
alternateReading: Paul voluntarily forgoes a right he recognizes, rather than rejecting the right itself.
limitation: Mission support must be distinguished from general household economic obligations.

title: Luke directs attention away from anxiety over material needs
observation: Luke directs attention away from anxiety over material needs; Paul urges quiet living and work.
alternateReading: Trust in divine care need not prohibit productive work or planning.
limitation: The relationship between mission circumstances and ordinary livelihood remains contextual.

title: Jesus challenges insulting anger
observation: Jesus challenges insulting anger; Paul warns against mutual destruction and urges blessing opponents.
alternateReading: Correction and strong criticism may be distinguished from hostile retaliation.
limitation: The exact boundaries of permissible rebuke require attention to context.

title: Luke relates speech to the heart
observation: Luke relates speech to the heart; Galatians contrasts destructive conduct with the Spirit's fruit.
alternateReading: The Gospel image and Paul's account of spiritual agency are not identical explanations.
limitation: The parallel concerns ethical disposition, not a complete shared psychology.

title: Jesus directs attention to divine care
observation: Jesus directs attention to divine care; Paul encourages prayer rather than anxiety.
alternateReading: Paul's promise of peace does not necessarily imply resolution of material hardship.
limitation: Neither text should be treated as a clinical treatment protocol for anxiety.

title: Luke emphasizes divine care and kingdom priorities
observation: Luke emphasizes divine care and kingdom priorities; Romans places suffering within future hope.
alternateReading: Different emphases may reflect distinct audiences and theological arguments rather than contradiction.
limitation: The relationship between present provision and future restoration needs further analysis.

title: The ability to repay an invitation
observation: Luke directs the host to invite guests who cannot repay, while naming resurrection as a horizon of recompense.
alternateReading: The instruction can be read as challenging the dominant motive for an invitation or as requiring a more radical replacement of the guest list.
limitation: The narrative does not record the host adopting either practice.

title: Unequal food and contested explanations
observation: Paul explicitly describes hunger, drunkenness and shaming. Kloppenborg disputes the inference that working hours explain late arrival.
alternateReading: Competitive allocation of portions is an alternative reconstruction informed by comparison with association meals.
limitation: Neither the assembly floor plan nor the arrival times are supplied in the letter.

title: Eating at home and opening the table
observation: Paul can direct a hungry participant to eat at home while Luke challenges a host to invite people who lack the means to reciprocate.
alternateReading: Paul may be restraining competitive private consumption at a communal rite. Luke addresses admission to a social meal.
limitation: A direct contradiction would require both instructions to apply to the same host, guests and meal.
